history.title: Crew Launch Week 9: Where Your Attention Goes

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Responsibility. "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."

This week is about who decides where your attention goes, and about setting one boundary that makes it you.

1. Read **Where Your Attention Goes** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Pulled or Chosen?** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Boundary, Ban, or Bait?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is about Nadia in math.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Digital Wellbeing Studio](#sel-hub/digitalWellbeing?station=sel_station_crew_launch_attention). Do the Self-Check honestly, then pick one habit from the Toolkit. Then open [Executive Function](#sel-hub/execfunction?station=sel_station_crew_launch_attention) and look at the Focus tab for one move that fits the class where your attention drifts most.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your boundary and what it beats.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Out of Sight, Not Just Out of Hand**.
9. Finish with the **Investigate Challenge: Where Did It Go?**, a three-day attention log.

Your commitment: this week, keep your phone in your bag (not your pocket) for one class every day, and notice the first time you reach for it. 🎒

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Where Your Attention Goes
history.data:
## Where Your Attention Goes

**HOWL: "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."**

The Responsibility **HOWL** asks you to participate fully and **mindfully**. Fully means you are in the room. In 2026 that is harder than it sounds, because there is a device in your pocket that was built, on purpose, by very smart people, to get you to pick it up. The red badge, the buzz, the **streak** that will break if you skip a day, the **autoplay** that starts the next video before you decide: none of that is an accident. Each one is a design **choice**, tested on millions of people, and kept because it worked.

This is not a lecture about phones being bad. Your phone is a tool, and a good one. The point is simpler: your **attention** is being **pulled** on purpose, and you should know it, so that where your attention goes is your choice and not someone else's.

Here is a moment from a fictional **Crew**. Nadia is in math, a class she is actually good at. Her phone is in her hoodie pocket. It buzzes. She does not take it out. But for the next three minutes, part of her is on the buzz: who was it, what did they say, is it about her. The teacher has moved on to the next example. Nadia **catches up**, but first she fell behind. She was in the room for the second example and not the first. Nobody saw her look at a phone. She still lost the minutes.

That is the part most people miss. The cost of a phone in class is not only the time you spend looking at it. It is the attention you spend not looking at it. Researchers have found that a buzz you do not answer still pulls your attention away for a while. Some studies suggest that even a silent phone on the desk takes a little attention, because part of you is keeping track of it. Out of sight does more than out of hand.

So this week is about **boundaries**, not **bans**. A ban is a rule someone else makes that takes the thing away completely. A boundary is a line you choose ahead of time, so that you do not have to decide in the moment when the buzz comes. Phone in the bag, not the pocket, for one class. **Notifications** off between 8 and 3. One set time to check, so the checking is a choice. The boundary does the work so willpower does not have to, which you may remember from the week on systems.

Being mindful, the other half of the HOWL, means noticing where your attention actually went, without judging it. This week you will investigate that. Not "was I good," but "where did it go, and what pulled it." The answer is information. What you do with it is responsibility.

questions.question: What does the reading say about the red badge, the buzz, and the streak?
options: They are accidents of how phones are built
They are design choices, tested and kept because they work
They only affect people who already use their phones too much
They were added because students asked for them
questions.correctAnswer: They are design choices, tested and kept because they work

questions.question: What is the reading's main point about phones?
options: Phones are bad and should be left at home
Teachers should collect every phone at the door before each class starts
Notifications are fine as long as you do not look at them
Where your attention goes should be your choice, not someone else's
questions.correctAnswer: Where your attention goes should be your choice, not someone else's

questions.question: Nadia did not take her phone out in math. What did it cost her anyway?
options: The three minutes part of her spent on the buzz, and the first example
Nothing, because nobody saw her look at it
A warning from the teacher for having it in her pocket
Her place in the class, because she fell behind for the whole period
questions.correctAnswer: The three minutes part of her spent on the buzz, and the first example

questions.question: What is the difference between a boundary and a ban, according to the reading?
options: A boundary is only for phones; a ban is for other things, like food
A boundary is stricter than a ban because you cannot argue with yourself
A boundary is a line you choose ahead of time; a ban comes from someone else
There is no real difference between them; both take the phone away
questions.correctAnswer: A boundary is a line you choose ahead of time; a ban comes from someone else

questions.question: What does "mindful" mean in this reading?
options: Feeling guilty when you check your phone during class
Meditating for ten minutes before each class
Keeping your mind on the teacher and pushing other thoughts out
Noticing where your attention went, without judging it
questions.correctAnswer: Noticing where your attention went, without judging it

questions.question: Name one thing your phone does on purpose to get you to pick it up, and one boundary that beats it.
questions.expectedAnswer: A tactic (notifications, red badges, autoplay, streaks) and a boundary (phone in the bag, notifications off for one class, a set check time).

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: My family needs to reach me during the day. Can I still have a boundary?
data.answer: Yes. A boundary is yours to shape. Most phones can let one or two contacts through while everything else is quiet. The boundary is on the pulls, not on your family.

data.question: Isn't this just a phone ban in disguise?
data.answer: No. A ban is someone else removing the phone. A boundary is you choosing a line, ahead of time, that you could change tomorrow. The reading says which one this week is.

data.question: What if I keep my phone in my bag and still cannot pay attention?
data.answer: Then the phone was not the only pull, and that is useful to know. The attention log in the challenge is for exactly that: finding out what actually pulls, which is sometimes hunger, sometimes worry, sometimes the person next to you.

data.question: Is it bad that the streak thing works on me?
data.answer: No. It works on almost everyone; that is why apps use it. Knowing it works on you is the first step to deciding whether to let it.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Responsibility HOWL says you participate fully and mindfully. Fully means you are in the room; mindfully means you notice where your attention went. Your teachers score HOWLs; Crew is where you practice them.

history.title: Investigate Challenge: Where Did It Go?

data.title: Where Did It Go?
data.instructions: For three school days, keep a private tally of the moments your attention left a class and what pulled it (phone, person, worry, hunger, boredom). Then set one boundary that matches the biggest pull and report the pattern, not the feelings.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behavior is participating fully and mindfully. A three-day log turns "pay attention" into an investigation with data the student owns, and the boundary that comes out of it is theirs, not a rule.

brief.context: Everyone has been told to pay attention. Almost nobody has been asked where attention actually goes when it leaves. You are going to find out, for yourself, over three days, with a tally small enough to keep on a sticky note.
brief.role: An investigator of your own attention
brief.audience: Yourself first; your Crew, which will hear the pattern and the boundary, not the private moments
brief.drivingQuestion: What pulls my attention out of class most often, and what one boundary would beat it?
brief.seedDirection: Pick three classes. Each time you notice your attention left, make one mark and a one-word note of the pull. At the end of three days, count the marks by pull. Set one boundary aimed at the biggest one. Try it for two more days.
lockedLessonFacts: The pulls in a phone are design choices, tested and kept because they work.
A buzz you do not answer still pulls your attention; some studies suggest even a silent phone on the desk takes a little.
A boundary is a line chosen ahead of time so you do not decide in the moment.
Mindful means noticing where attention went, without judging it.
openQuestions: Is my biggest pull the phone, or something else?
What time of day do the marks cluster?
Which boundary matches the pull, not just the phone?
What would I change after two days with the boundary?
stakeholders: The teacher of the class with the most marks
A family member who needs to reach you
criteria: At least three days of tally with a pull named for each mark
The counts are honest, including a big number
The boundary matches the biggest pull
The report gives the pattern, not the feelings
Uses at least three glossary words
constraints: Marks stay private; only the counts are shared
The boundary is set ahead of time, with a when and a where
Two days of testing before the report
brief.deliverable: A half-page report: the tally by pull, the boundary chosen and why, and what two days with it were like.

parallelExample.context: A fictional student expected the phone to be the biggest pull.
parallelExample.move: After three days the tally was: phone 6, the person next to me 9, hungry 4. The boundary was to move seats in one class. The phone boundary came second.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the investigation can change the answer; the boundary follows the data, not the assumption.

supports.frameStarter: Over three days my attention left class ____ times. The biggest pull was ____ (____ marks). My boundary is ____, set on ____.
frameChoices: After two days with the boundary, ____.
coachPrompts: Is your boundary aimed at your biggest pull or at the pull you expected?
What would make your tally more honest?

data.coachHint: Students may under-count to look good. Say out loud that a big number is a good investigation, not a bad student.
data.sourceExcerpt: Being mindful means noticing where your attention actually went, without judging it. Not "was I good," but "where did it go, and what pulled it." The answer is information.
